methodology.scope: The initial denominator combines the dominant volume resins with established engineering thermoplastics, thermosets, elastomers, fibers, natural and semisynthetic polymers, degradable and biomedical materials, and a representative functional-polymer tail. Families and processing-relevant subfamilies may both appear because they answer different research questions.
selectionSignals: Documented presence among dominant global resin groups
Repeated treatment in open polymer textbooks or university courseware
Distinct industrial processing, cure, spinning, or vulcanization behavior
Established engineering, high-temperature, barrier, elastomeric, biomedical, or functional use
Recognized polymer class or source-based name in public nomenclature references
methodology.rankingDisclaimer: This is a curated high-priority coverage set, not a quantitative worldwide production ranking. Public market sources resolve the largest resin groups but aggregate much of the long tail.

sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis:
High-density polyethylene is made from ethylene by coordination-polymerization routes that limit chain branching. In the Ziegler–Natta route described by OpenStax, an alkylaluminum and titanium compound generate an alkyltitanium active site; ethylene coordinates to the metal and inserts into the growing metal–carbon bond. Repetition gives a predominantly linear polyethylene chain. This mechanism describes one important catalyst family, not every catalyst platform used for HDPE.

A 1976 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency process survey documented solution-, slurry-, and vapor-phase reactor classes for HDPE. Its historical examples contrasted a supported chromium-oxide route with a titanium/aluminum Ziegler route, described small hydrogen or telogen additions as chain-length controls, and placed monomer and solvent recovery, stripping, and drying after polymerization. Those examples establish industrial route diversity but are not a current universal recipe or a claim that the named conditions remain dominant.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Close packing of comparatively linear polyethylene chains creates crystalline regions with strong interchain dispersion interactions. Crystallinity, crystal orientation, molecular architecture, and processing-induced orientation therefore affect stiffness, yield, strength, and toughness; HDPE does not have one context-free mechanical-property set.

Amjadi and Fatemi tested virgin, regrind, and multilayer HDPE specimens prepared from compression-, injection-, and blow-molded plaques. Their tensile program used ASTM D638 and ISO 527 geometries across 1, 2, and 4 mm thicknesses, temperatures from −40 to 82 °C, and several loading rates. For the material and process subsets varied in that program, modulus and tensile strength decreased as temperature increased and rose with strain rate. At 23 °C and a strain rate of 6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, the paper reports for its unnamed virgin injection-molded material that increasing specimen thickness from 2 to 4 mm raised elastic modulus by 23% while reducing ultimate tensile strength by about 21%; the same thickness effect was not observed for its compression-molded sets. The paper does not identify a commercial grade or conditioning protocol, and its Figure 3 does not report test direction or a sample count. These findings are specimen- and process-specific rather than family-wide constants.

A separate INEOS grade table illustrates formulation spread under defined tests. At 23 °C, HD4620BM, HD6030BM, and HD6070EA list tensile moduli of 950, 1500, and 1500 MPa by ISO 527-2 on machined specimens from pressed plates, with corresponding notched Charpy impact values of 9, 5, and 4 kJ/m² by ISO 179-1. The table does not state conditioning, and it gives no Charpy specimen-preparation detail beyond notching. These are typical vendor values for named grades, not specification limits or an HDPE family range, and they should not be directly merged with values from differently prepared molded articles.
sections.processing:
HDPE is converted by extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, and compression molding. The selected route is part of the resulting material state: flow-induced orientation, cooling history, plaque or wall thickness, and repeated thermal history can change crystallinity and tensile response. Process selection and mechanical design therefore need to be evaluated together for the intended grade and article.

INEOS publishes suggested injection-molding starting conditions for its O&P HDPE resins, grouped by nominal melt-flow rate. For the four listed melt-flow bands of 2–6, 6–11, 11–25, and 25–45 g/10 min, the respective melt-temperature starts are 430 ± 10, 420 ± 10, 410 ± 10, and 400 ± 10 °F. The same sheet gives a 50–70 °F mold-temperature range and 800–1500 psi first-stage injection pressure, states that predrying is not normally necessary for these resins, and recommends systematic adjustment to balance cycle time, part quality, and performance. It warns that excessive or insufficient melt temperature and pressure can produce flash, burning, sink, warpage, voids, poor surfaces, short shots, or molded-in stress. These are vendor starting conditions for the covered resin set, not a universal HDPE window.

sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyamide 6 is produced from the six-carbon lactam ε-caprolactam by ring-opening polymerization, but published routes should not be collapsed into one recipe. In the water-initiated description, a small amount of water hydrolyzes part of the caprolactam to 6-aminohexanoic acid; amino-group addition to further caprolactam then propagates the chain, with heating producing nylon 6. A distinct anionic ring-opening route uses a strong non-nucleophilic base and often a lactam-derived imide co-initiator or an acylating agent. Varghese and Grinstaff report early industrial water-catalyzed polymerization at 240–280 °C and later activated anionic methods that increased rate and reduced residual monomer. The water-initiated and anhydrous strong-base descriptions are alternative synthesis regimes, not conditions to combine.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Interchain hydrogen bonding between PA6 amide groups contributes to its mechanical response, but measured values remain grade-, preparation-, conditioning-, and test-specific rather than PA6 constants. Zheng and co-workers used UBE Nylon 1022B as the neat-PA6 control in an open study: the starting pellets were vacuum-dried at 110 °C overnight, tensile dumbbells were injection-molded to ISO 527-2-5A, and tests were run at 25 °C and 5 mm/min. They report a yield strength of 63.0 MPa and Young's modulus of 1258.7 MPa. The cited methods and figure do not state post-molding conditioning or a replicate/statistical basis. Nylene describes NX1440 as a nucleated, medium-viscosity nylon 6 molding grade and reports, on dry-as-molded specimens at 22.8 °C, ASTM D638 tensile strength of 83 MPa and elongation at break of 25%, ASTM D790 flexural modulus of 2759 MPa, and ASTM D256 notched Izod impact of 43 J/m. Its table does not identify specimen geometry or a replicate/statistical basis. These ISO and ASTM results use different grades, specimen preparation, conditioning descriptions, and endpoints, so they should not be averaged or presented as a family-wide range.
sections.processing: Processing conditions differ materially across grades, formulations, equipment, and intended articles. In an open laboratory study that used UBE Nylon 1022B as the neat-PA6 control for PA6/ionic-liquid blends, Zheng and co-workers vacuum-dried the starting PA6 pellets at 110 °C overnight, mixed material at 220 °C for 2 min at 20 rpm followed by 5 min at 50 rpm, and hot-pressed 500 µm films at 230 °C and 10 MPa for 3 min before cooling under the same pressure; tensile dumbbells were separately injection-molded to ISO 527-2-5A. These are experimental specimen-preparation conditions, not a general PA6 processing recommendation. For BASF Ultramid B3K6, identified only as glass-sphere-filled PA6-GB30, the processing sheet recommends 0.03–0.06% moisture, dry-air drying at 80 °C for 4 h, a 270–290 °C melt range, an 80–90 °C mould range, and at most 10 min residence. It notes that drying time depends on initial moisture, drying temperature, and dryer dew point, that poor storage can require longer drying, and that excessive drying may increase melt viscosity. Nylene's page places separate guidance under the heading 'PA6 Injection Molding - Unreinforced': less than 0.20% moisture after 2–4 h at 66–82 °C, a 227–293 °C melt range depending on residence time and shot size, a 49–93 °C mould range, and preferably no more than 6 min residence, shorter at higher melt temperature. Neither supplier states the basis, measurement point, or method for its moisture percentage. The designator PA6-GB30 is not decoded into a filler mass fraction without separate evidence. These windows remain source-specific examples, not a combined PA6-family processing window.
